meta.title: Who really said "If people don't want to come out to the ballpark, nobody's going to stop them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yogi Berra said a version of it — but impresario Sol Hurok was quoted with the joke in 1952, ten years before it was first linked to Berra.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If people don't want to come out to the ballpark, nobody's going to stop them'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Yogi original. Sol Hurok was quoted with the joke in 1952; Berra's ballpark version first surfaces in 1962.

answer.label: Not originally Yogi Berra — the joke starts with Sol Hurok
answer.sourceLine: The gag was already in print in 1952, when columnist Leonard Lyons quoted the concert impresario Sol Hurok: “If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” Yogi Berra did say a baseball version of it — the earliest citation linking it to him is from 1962 — and he later printed his own wording in a 2001 book, but he did not invent the joke.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed: Berra popularized a ballpark version, but the line is documented earlier from Sol Hurok.

source.trailTitle: How a showman’s line became a baseball line
trail: 1952 — Leonard Lyons’ column of August 16 quotes Sol Hurok: “If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” Quote Investigator ↗
1959 — LIFE magazine of June 1 runs a Hurok profile, “Impresario Who Booked the Bolshoi,” carrying the line again as “When people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” Quote Investigator ↗

1962–1964 — Joe Garagiola tells banquet audiences that Yogi said it about Kansas City; the 1964 Boston Record American version reads “Those fans in Kansas City don’t want to come out and see their ball club—and nobody is gonna stop ’em.” Quote Investigator ↗
2001 — Berra prints his own wording in When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It!, written with Dave Kaplan — the closest published match to the phrasing that circulates today. Publisher page ↗
source.excerptNote: Sol Hurok, warning the producers of the film Tonight We Sing, as quoted by Leonard Lyons in 1952. The ballpark noun and the “nobody’s going to stop them” ending arrive later, with Berra.

author.name: Sol Hurok
author.kicker: The man who actually said it first
author.heading: Who was Sol Hurok?
author.bio: Sol Hurok was the twentieth century’s most famous concert impresario — the man behind the “S. Hurok Presents” billing that carried Marian Anderson, Arthur Rubinstein, Feodor Chaliapin and Van Cliburn to American stages. Born in the Russian Empire in 1888, he emigrated in 1906 and became a naturalised American in 1914. He arranged Anderson’s landmark 1939 Lincoln Memorial concert and brought the Bolshoi Ballet to the United States in 1959, and he talked about box office with the fatalism of a man who had spent fifty years selling tickets.

Chronology per Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: If People Don’t Want to Come, Nothing Will Stop Them,” October 30, 2014.

copyAttribution: Sol Hurok, quoted by Leonard Lyons in The Post-Standard (Syracuse, NY), 16 August 1952: "If people don't want to come, nothing will stop them." The ballpark version — "If people don't want to come out to the park, nobody's going to stop them" — is Yogi Berra's later adaptation, first linked to him in 1962 and printed in his 2001 book "When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It!"

misattribution.heading: Berra repeated it. Hurok said it first.
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication — Yogi Berra really did say a version of this line, more than once, and put one in his own book. It is a priority problem: the joke was already circulating under someone else’s name.

items.why: The earliest citation tying the quip to Berra is a 1962 report of Joe Garagiola’s banquet speech, quoting Yogi on sagging Kansas City attendance: “If they don’t want to come out, nobody’s gonna stop ’em.” Berra printed his own version in 2001, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Leonard Lyons’ column of August 16, 1952 quotes the impresario: “I’m enough of a showman to have learned at least this: If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” A 1959 LIFE profile carries the same line, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Berra’s childhood friend and fellow catcher was the one telling the story from banquet podiums in 1962 and explaining it in print in 1963 — the mechanism by which a showman’s line became a baseball line, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the thought and the wording belong to Sol Hurok in 1952; Berra moved it to the ballpark and made it famous. Wikiquote files it under Disputed ↗ for exactly this reason.

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting pinned on Yogi
lead: Yogi Berra is one of the internet’s great quote magnets, and he knew it: he liked to say he never said everything he said. Attendance jokes are exactly the kind of thing that drifts toward him, because the shape of the line — a sentence that sounds like a tautology until you hear the shrug inside it — is the shape of every Yogi-ism.

But this one had a previous owner. Sol Hurok spent half a century selling seats for singers and ballet companies, and the fatalism is his: you can advertise, you can beg, you cannot make people show up. What Berra did was move it from the concert hall to the ballpark — in the 1960s citations, specifically to the thin crowds in Kansas City.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology runs: Leonard Lyons’ column of August 16, 1952 (Hurok, “If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them”); LIFE magazine, June 1, 1959, in a Hurok profile titled “Impresario Who Booked the Bolshoi” (“When people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them”); then, in 1962, Joe Garagiola telling a banquet audience that his friend Yogi had said, of Kansas City’s attendance, “If they don’t want to come out, nobody’s gonna stop ’em.”

The 1964 Boston Record American version is longer and more explicitly about Kansas City: “Those fans in Kansas City don’t want to come out and see their ball club—and nobody is gonna stop ’em.” The clipped modern wording — the one on the mugs — is closest to the form Berra himself printed in 2001.
context.pull: You can advertise, you can beg. You cannot make people show up.
